variation.original_summary: Mariáš is a Czech three-player trick-taking game with a 32-card deck. A declarer picks trump and a contract and plays against two defenders who are partners. Players must follow suit, head the trick and trump when void. Aces and Tens are worth 10 each, the last trick is worth 10, and marriages add points. Flek and re double the stakes, and there are special contracts (Betl, Durch, Seven, Hundred).

review.evidence: No simple policy wins. Always declaring loses against weak hands, and always passing gives up every strong hand. Flek every time pays double whenever the declarer makes the contract. The forehand advantage is balanced over a full rotation. Choices of trump, contract and card play decide most deals.
Over many deals strong players beat weak ones reliably, through card counting, partnership defence and judging when to bid or flek. Any single deal is heavily card-driven.
The game is deep and unsolved: inferring hands from play, defensive signalling, bid judgment and doubling psychology. A beginner who follows suit and bids only strong hands still scores.
Hands are hidden. Players must infer cards from the bidding and from voids shown in play, and plan over 10 tricks. Defenders must also cooperate without seeing each other's cards.
Card points, marriages and contract success are all arithmetic, and the stakes follow from the multipliers.

Ten tricks with must-head rules, a talon exchange, marriages, four special contracts and sequential flek/re chains exceed the step and choice limits. The previous built version crashed five times: drawing from an emptied deck, empty list searches for the trick winner, and unfilled {held} placeholders. It also showed empty bookkeeping fields to players.

problems: P1: The full rules (32 cards, 10 tricks, talon exchange, marriages, Betl/Durch/Seven/Hundred) need far more steps and choices per round than the engine allows.
P2: Dealing by repeated random index draws from a shrinking deck crashed with 'list index out of range' when the deck ran short or was not rebuilt.
P3: Finding the trick winner by searching the trick list afterwards crashed with empty list comprehensions.
P4: The 'must head the trick' duty and the illegal-card fallback made each play step hard to validate, and could produce a card that never landed in the trick.
P5: Prompts embedded a {held} placeholder that the engine cannot fill, so players saw literal braces.
P6: Internal bookkeeping fields (deal_result, last_card, trump before it was set) were printed empty to players.
P7: The forehand who must name trump has a built-in edge or burden within a deal, so balance needs even rotation.
P8: A sequential flek, then re, then further doubling chain costs several choice steps.

changes.what: Shrink the deck to 12 cards: four suits (Hearts, Bells, Leaves, Acorns) times three ranks (A, 10, K). Deal 4 cards each with no talon, for 4 tricks per deal. Drop marriages and the special contracts. Card values stay A=10 and 10=10, and the last trick stays 10, so the total is still 90.
changes.why: This keeps the 90-point economy, the trump choice and follow/trump play, while one trick fits in one round with at most 4 choice steps.

changes.what: At the start of each deal, build a fresh list of the 12 card codes 0 to 11 and shuffle it once. Seat 1 takes positions 1-4, seat 2 positions 5-8, seat 3 positions 9-12. There are no index draws from a shrinking deck.
changes.why: A fixed-size permutation sliced at fixed positions cannot run out, and it is the round's only random draw.

changes.what: Track the trick winner with a running best_key and best_seat. The leader's card sets them. Each later card replaces them only if its key is strictly greater. The key is rank (K=0, 10=1, A=2), plus 10 if trump, plus 5 if of the led suit.
changes.why: No list search is needed, so nothing can come back empty.

changes.what: Use plain follow-suit: follow the led suit if able, otherwise trump if able, otherwise any card. An illegal or unheld card is replaced by the lowest-code legal card. A hand always has a card when its owner plays.
changes.why: Each play is one validated step, and the played card always exists and always enters the trick.

changes.what: Prompts contain no placeholders except {seat} and {value}. Each player's own hand is shown through their private hand attribute in their state view.

Hide the bookkeeping attributes (best_key, led_suit, deck, the bid's raw fields). Show only hand, score, trump, declarer, contract, multiplier, cards in the current trick, trick number and the points taken so far.
changes.why: The state view holds only usable information.

changes.what: Play 9 deals, with the eldest hand rotating 1, 2, 3, 1, ... so each seat is eldest exactly 3 times. The eldest cannot pass: an invalid entry or PASS from the eldest counts as '50 A'. Bid ties go to the player nearest the eldest in seat order.
changes.why: This preserves Mariáš's forced forehand while spreading that burden and privilege evenly.

changes.what: Make flek and re one simultaneous poll after trick 1. Each defender says FLEK or NO, and the declarer says RE or NO at the same moment. Any flek doubles the stake. RE doubles it again only if at least one flek was given.
changes.why: One choice step replaces a sequential chain, and the declarer must predict whether the defenders will flek.

variation.name: Malý Mariáš (Little Mariáš)
variation.summary: A 12-card, 4-trick Mariáš for three players over 9 deals. Each deal, players bid in secret for the right to declare a trump suit and a card-point target out of 90. The two others defend together. Flek and re double the stakes, Hearts doubles them again, and the highest running total after 9 deals wins.
variation.rules:
CARDS. There are 12 cards: four suits, Hearts (H), Bells (B), Leaves (L) and Acorns (A), each with three ranks, Ace (A), Ten (10) and King (K). A card is written rank then suit, for example AH, 10L, KB. Internally, card code = 3 x suit index + rank index, with suits H=0, B=1, L=2, A=3 and ranks K=0, 10=1, A=2. Rank order within a suit is A > 10 > K. Card points: each Ace 10, each Ten 10, each King 0. Whoever wins the 4th (last) trick of a deal gets 10 more. The total per deal is 90.

STRUCTURE. The match is 9 deals of 4 tricks each, which is 36 rounds. Each round is one trick. The eldest hand of deal d is seat ((d-1) mod 3)+1, so seats 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3. Every player starts with score 0.

WHAT PLAYERS SEE. Each player sees their own hand (private), all scores, the current deal and trick number, the declarer, contract and trump once set, the stake multiplier, the cards played so far in the current trick with who played them, the card points taken so far by the declarer and by the defenders, and every public announcement. Internal working values are not shown.

ROUND STEPS (steps marked [trick 1] or [trick 2] happen only in that trick of a deal):
1. [trick 1] Deal. Build the list of the 12 codes 0-11, shuffle it once, and give positions 1-4 to seat 1, positions 5-8 to seat 2 and positions 9-12 to seat 3. Reset the declarer points, defender points and multiplier to 1.
2. [trick 1] Bid (simultaneous, secret). Each player answers 'PASS' or 'N S', where N is 50, 60, 70, 80 or 90 and S is H, B, L or A. The eldest may not pass: PASS or any invalid answer from the eldest counts as '50 A'. An invalid answer from anyone else counts as PASS.
3. [trick 1] Resolve the bid. The highest N becomes the declarer, with contract N and trump S. On a tie, the tied player first in seat order starting from the eldest wins. The other two are defenders. Set base stake = N/10 - 4 (so 50→1, 60→2, 70→3, 80→4, 90→5). The declarer leads trick 1. Announce all bids, the declarer, the contract and the trump.
4. [trick 2] Flek poll (simultaneous). Each defender answers FLEK or NO, and the declarer answers RE or NO. Invalid answers count as NO.
5. [trick 2] Resolve. If at least one defender said FLEK, the multiplier is doubled. If, in addition, the declarer said RE, it is doubled again. Announce all answers and the multiplier.
6. First card. The leader names a card from their hand.
7. Resolve the first card. If the card is not in the leader's hand, the lowest-code card in their hand is played instead. Remove it from the hand and add it to the trick. Set led suit to its suit. Set best_key = rank index + (10 if its suit is trump) + 5, and set best_seat = the leader. Announce the card.
8. Second card. The next seat clockwise, (leader mod 3)+1, names a card.
9. Resolve the second card. The card is legal if: it is of the led suit; or the hand has no led-suit card and the card is trump; or the hand has neither led-suit cards nor trumps. If the named card is not held or not legal, play instead the lowest-code held card of the led suit, else the lowest-code held trump, else the lowest-code held card. Remove the card from the hand and add it to the trick. Its key = rank index + (10 if trump) + (5 if of the led suit). If its key is greater than best_key, set best_key to it and best_seat to this seat. Announce the card.
10. Third card. The next seat names a card.
11. Resolve the third card exactly as in step 9.
12. Award the trick. Add the trick's card points, plus 10 if this is trick 4, to the declarer's points if best_seat is the declarer, otherwise to the defenders' points. Set leader = best_seat. Announce the winner and the running points.
13. [trick 4] Settle the deal. Stake = base stake x multiplier x (2 if trump is Hearts, else 1). If the declarer's points are at least the contract N, the declarer gains 2 x stake and each defender loses stake. Otherwise the declarer loses 2 x stake and each defender gains stake. Announce the result and the scores.
14. Advance. Add 1 to the trick number. After trick 4, reset it to 1, add 1 to the deal number and rotate the eldest. After deal 9, the match ends.

There is no discussion phase. Hands are always non-empty when their owner must play, because each player plays exactly one card per trick and holds 4 cards for 4 tricks.
variation.objective: After 9 deals, the player with the highest score wins. If two or three players tie for highest, those players draw. Scores are the sum of the zero-sum deal settlements in step 13.
variation.expected_effect: Bidding becomes a real judgment: hand strength, choice of trump, the risk of a Hearts contract and the stake level. The forced eldest must handle weak hands, which is spread evenly by rotation. The simultaneous flek/re poll rewards reading hand strength from the bids. Defenders must cooperate within a deal through card play alone (they read each other's discards and voids), while remaining rivals for the overall win, since both gain or lose equally in a deal but only one can finish first. Card counting over 4 tricks with 12 known cards rewards inference: by trick 3 a careful player can often deduce the remaining hands exactly. Simple policies all lose. Always passing leaves the eldest stuck with forced 50s and gives up strong hands. Always bidding 90 fails most deals at the maximum stake. Always flekking pays double whenever the declarer bid soundly. Always re-ing costs the declarer double whenever a flekked contract fails. Deal luck stays, but 9 deals and the freedom to bid low or pass let good players limit its effect. Talk is left out: the only conflict within a deal is declarer against defenders, and public talk between the defenders would reveal their hands to the declarer as well.

balanced.evidence:
Deal settlement table (s = base stake x multiplier x 2 if trump is Hearts): declarer makes the contract: declarer +2s, each defender -s. Declarer fails: declarer -2s, each defender +s. Every deal sums to zero. Base stake is 1/2/3/4/5 for bids 50/60/70/80/90, the multiplier is 1, 2 or 4, so s ranges from 1 to 40. Declarer expected value is 2s(2p-1), where p is the chance of making the contract.

The point total checks: 4 Aces (40) + 4 Tens (40) + last trick (10) = 90. The trick keys order correctly: an off-suit non-trump card scores 0-2, a led-suit non-trump 5-7, an off-led trump 10-12, and a led trump 15-17. So trump beats led suit, and a discard never wins.

Thoughtless policies under the WINNER RULE:
(a) Always '90 H' (the highest bid). This player declares almost every deal. Contract 90 needs every point card and the last trick, so a defender winning any trick that holds a point card breaks it. That is near-certain failure: -2x5x2 = -20 per deal, or -40 to -80 if the defenders Flek. This loses to sensible and to random play.
(b) Always PASS / NO / lowest card. As eldest this player is forced into '50 A', with Acorns trump whatever the hand, three times. As defender it pays s whenever a sensible opponent bids a strong hand and makes it. It gains when random opponents overbid, but a sensible player gains those too, and sensible play also takes its own strong hands. It does not avoid losses against sensible play.
(c) Always FLEK. This is not dominant. It doubles a loss whenever p > 0.5, which is likely when the declarer is a non-eldest who chose to bid.

No option wins whatever the opponents do. A sample strong hand, AH 10H AB KL with Hearts trump, lands around 50-60 points, so 50 is reachable with a good hand but not with an average forced eldest hand. Bidding therefore needs a real valuation.

Seat balance: eldest, including its tie-break priority and its forced bid, rotates 1,2,3 x3, so each seat is eldest exactly 3 times. The play order is fixed relative to the declarer and is not tied to a seat number. All three players can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
Rules coverage: every situation is defined.
- Invalid bids default: the eldest to '50 A', others to PASS.
- Bid ties break in seat order from the eldest.
- Illegal or unheld cards are replaced by a fixed rule: led suit first, then trump, then any card, lowest code.
- Follow-suit and must-trump are enforced arithmetically through the key. 'Must head' is dropped consistently.
- Flek/Re resolution, the settlement formula and the tie-draw winner rule are all stated.
- Hands always hold enough cards: 4 cards for 4 tricks.
- The game is finite: 9 deals x 4 tricks = 36 rounds.

Limits:
- 14 steps per round (limit 20).
- 4 choices per round (limit 4). Trick 1 has bid + 3 cards. Trick 2 has Flek + 3 cards. Tricks 3-4 have 3 cards.
- Attribute count is about 18 (limit 20): deal, trick, eldest, declarer, contract, trump, base stake, multiplier, declarer points, defender points, leader, led suit, best_key, best_seat, trick cards, plus scores.
- 2 hidden elements: hands and secret bids (limit 3).
- 1 shuffle, in trick 1 only (limit 1).
- No board, judge or clock.
- Simultaneous decisions (bids, Flek) are polls. Card play is sequential, as trick order requires.
- The deck is handled by list shuffle and removal, which is a supported workaround.

Talk: omitting it is sensible. The only aligned pair is the defenders, and public talk would hand their information to the declarer. Inference from bids and card play is the intended channel.

The game is not a fixed-length cooperation dilemma, so there is no late-round 'safe option' collapse.

triage.reason: The tests match the rules: a trump beats the Ace of the led suit, a player void in the led suit must trump and overtrump, and a player with neither may play any card. The game breaks all of these, which points to faulty trump handling in the file, not to a test or rule problem. The game also credits too many points to declarer_points in the trump-marriage scenario.
triage.guidance:
1) Trump detection. `trump` is stored as text ('Hearts'), but card suits come from code/5 as numbers 0-3. Convert the trump to its suit index (via suit_names/suit_indices) once at bidding and keep it in a table attribute such as trump_index. Compare floor(card/suit_code_multiplier) against that index everywhere.
2) Trick winner. Give each card the key rank + trump_key_bonus if its suit is the trump index + led_suit_key_bonus if its suit is the led suit (the suit of the leader's card). The highest key wins.
3) Legal-card offers. A player holding the led suit must play it, and must beat the highest led-suit card already in the trick if they can. That beating duty is lifted only if the led suit is not trump and a trump is already in the trick. A player void in the led suit who holds a trump must play a trump, and must beat the highest trump in the trick if they can. A player holding neither may play any card in hand. Build the offer list from these three cases. Apply the fallback (the lowest-rank legal card, ties by suit order) only to that legal set.
4) Points. declarer_points must hold card points only: Aces and Tens plus last_trick_bonus, added once on trick 6. Do not add marriage values, and do not add the last-trick 10 twice. Marriages go into the tally only at the end of the deal, using declarer_marriages/defender_marriages and the min_tricks_for_marriages check.

triage.reason: Several independent trick-play scenarios fail in the same way: the trick points go to the wrong side, a trump does not beat a led-suit Ace, the trick winner does not lead next, and a seat is offered a card the follow and overtrump rules forbid. The tests match the written rules, so the game file's legal-card filtering, trick-winner calculation and point crediting are wrong.
triage.guidance:
1) Legal cards: build each later player's offer list exactly as the rules say. If the player holds the led suit, offer only that suit, and among it only cards that beat the highest led-suit card already played if any can. Lift that beating duty only when the led suit is not trump and a trump is already in the trick. Otherwise, if the player holds a trump, offer only trumps, and only those beating the highest trump in the trick if any can. Otherwise offer the whole hand. The fallback for an illegal or missing card is the legal card of lowest rank, ties broken Hearts, Bells, Leaves, Acorns.
2) Trick winner: give each card in the trick a key of rank (code % 5), plus trump_key_bonus if its suit (floor(code/5)) equals trump, plus led_suit_key_bonus if its suit equals the leader's suit. Map the position of the highest key back to the seat that played it. Seats play in cyclic order starting from the leader, so position i is seat ((leader-1+i)%3)+1, not seat i+1.
3) Crediting: compare the winning seat with `declarer`. Add the trick's card points (ace_points or ten_points per card, plus last_trick_bonus only on trick 6, added once) to `declarer_points` if they are equal and to `defender_points` otherwise. Add 1 to the declarer's tricks only when the declarer wins. Set the leader to the winning seat.
4) Keep marriages out of `declarer_points` and `defender_points`. They enter only the end-of-deal tally, subject to min_tricks_for_marriages. Check that trick 6 is not credited twice and the bonus is not added twice, since the marriage scenario shows `declarer_points` 10 too high.

triage.reason: Across five attempts the coder fixed each reported problem, yet the match kept crashing in the card-handling core. The trick-winner calculation failed twice (attempts 3 and 5) and the deck draw once, which points to legality, fallback and trick bookkeeping too intricate to build reliably on a flat step list. The repeated failures, rather than one fixable slip, suggest the design itself should be simplified.
triage.guidance:
Simplify the trick mechanics so each play step is easy to validate and record.

1. Drop the 'must beat' duty in (a) and (b). Keep plain follow-suit: follow the led suit if able, otherwise trump if able, otherwise any card.
2. Replace the illegal-card fallback with a simple rule, such as 'the first legal card in your hand in code order', so the played card always exists and always lands in the trick list.
3. State that the trick winner is the card with the highest key (rank + 10 if trump + 5 if led suit), and the seat that played it. Record the winning seat directly while the cards are played: keep a running best key and best seat updated after each card, rather than searching the trick list afterwards.
4. Say explicitly that the full 20-card deck is rebuilt and reshuffled at the start of every deal.
5. Simplify the invalid-suit default for bidding to a fixed suit (for example the suit of the player's first card, or Acorns), rather than the suit with the most cards.
6. Consider dropping marriages, or limiting them to the trump suit only, to cut announcement and tally steps.

Keep the scoring formula, which is sound and zero-sum.

triage.reason: The rules are sound and the tests read them correctly. The game never offered the flek poll options, so each player's `offer` list stayed empty, every answer defaulted to NO and the multiplier stayed at 1. Per-seat options in a simultaneous poll are within the platform's capabilities, so this is an implementation error.
triage.guidance: At trick 2, before the flek poll step, fill each player's `offer` attribute: the declarer gets ['RE', 'NO'] and each defender gets ['FLEK', 'NO']. Use per-operation `if` conditions comparing the seat with table `declarer`. Make sure this fill runs in the same round as the poll, before it, and is not cleared or overwritten first. Then make the poll a single simultaneous choice that draws its options from `offer`. In the resolve step, count FLEK answers from the defenders. If there is at least one, multiply `multiplier` by `flek_factor`. If, in addition, the declarer answered RE, multiply it by `re_factor`. Announce all three answers and the multiplier. Also check that `trump_name` is updated when the trump is set (it still says 'not chosen yet'), and that the hand arrays hold 4 cards per seat (`cards_per_hand`), not 3.

triage.reason: The game was built as specified, and evaluation shows two design flaws. Each round has five choice steps (bid, flek poll, three cards), over the limit of four. A thoughtless first-option policy, which most likely amounts to always passing and never fleking, wins about 95% of matches, while the last option (always bidding the highest contract) almost always loses. Bidding as designed punishes declaring far more than it rewards it.
triage.guidance:
1) Bring each round to at most 4 choice steps. Simplest: drop the flek/re poll, or fold it into the bid answer (for example 'N S' only, multiplier fixed at 1). The three card plays plus the bid then make 4.
2) Rebalance bidding so that passing is not a free, dominant default and overbidding is not suicidal:
- Narrow the contract range to what is realistically makeable out of 90 points, for example 50, 60 or 70 only.
- Make the declarer's gain and loss symmetric (1x each instead of 2x stake against 2 defenders paying 1x), or reward a made contract by more than a failure costs.
- Consider forcing a declarer every deal so passing cannot simply dodge risk. The eldest already defaults; you could also give the declarer a small bonus for taking the contract.
- Drop the Hearts doubling unless it is shown to be balanced.
3) Check that, against random opponents, neither always-first nor always-last options win a large majority. The option order for bids and cards should not encode a dominant strategy (for example, lowest card code always safe, or PASS always first).
